screens.heading: Who owns this address?

teacher.say: Tap each part of the address. Only one part tells you who really owns the site.

body: A web address is built from parts, and attackers rely on you reading it too quickly. Tap each part of this fake address to see what it means.

parts.label: Protocol
parts.note: This says the connection is encrypted. It says nothing about who runs the site.

parts.label: Subdomain labels
parts.note: Everything in front of the main domain is chosen freely by whoever owns that domain. Here the attacker has placed a trusted-looking name in front. It is decoration.

parts.label: Domain
parts.note: Read from the right and stop at the first single slash. The last name there is the owner. This site belongs to account-check.net, not to examplebank.com. For endings like .co.uk, the owner is the name just before that ending.

parts.label: Path
parts.note: Anything after the first single slash is just a page on that site. The owner can name it anything, including a bank's name.

screens.key_takeaway: Read the address from the right, up to the first single slash. That last name tells you who owns the site.

screens.heading: Tricks in the address

teacher.say: Fake addresses work because they look right at a glance. Read them slowly.

body: Attackers register thousands of addresses that resemble well-known ones. These are the most common tricks.

points.label: Lookalike characters
points.text: examp1ebank.com uses the number 1 in place of the letter l, and the letters rn can pass for an m. Read letter by letter.

points.label: Extra words
points.text: Names like examplebank-secure.com or examplebank-login.net are not the bank. Real companies rarely add words such as secure or verify to their main domain.

points.label: A different ending
points.text: examplebank.co and examplebank.help are different sites from examplebank.com.

points.label: Lookalike alphabets
points.text: Some addresses use letters from other alphabets that look identical to ours. Typing the address yourself avoids the risk.

points.label: Hidden destinations
points.text: Shortened links and QR codes hide the address. Preview it before you open it, or skip it.

screens.key_takeaway: Fake addresses win by looking right at a glance. Slow down and read every character.

screens.heading: Real or fake?

teacher.say: Both pages below show a padlock. Press the button to see what really gives the fake away.

body: A convincing fake can be built in minutes. Compare a real sign-in page with a fake one, then reveal the differences.

fake.banner: Session expired. Sign in again within 5 minutes.

differences.label: The address
differences.text: examplebank-login.com is not examplebank.com. A different domain means a different owner.

differences.label: The pressure
differences.text: A banner says the session expired and demands an immediate sign-in. Real banks do not rush you through a link.

differences.label: The extra request
differences.text: The fake page also asks for the card PIN. A genuine sign-in page never needs it.

differences.label: The padlock
differences.text: Both pages have one. It only means the connection is encrypted.

differences.label: How you got there
differences.text: You reached the fake page through a message. You should reach the real one yourself.

screens.key_takeaway: The padlock does not prove a site is real. The address and the context do.

screens.heading: Safe habits for websites

teacher.say: A few small habits make fake sites almost useless against you.

body: You do not need to inspect every address under a microscope. A few habits remove most of the risk.

points.label: Bookmark or type
points.text: Reach banks, email and work systems through a bookmark or by typing the address, not through links in messages.

points.label: Let your password manager decide
points.text: A password manager fills a login only on the exact address it saved. If it stays silent on a page that looks right, treat that as a warning.

points.label: Respect browser warnings
points.text: A full-page warning about a deceptive site is serious. Close the page instead of clicking through.

points.label: Be wary of expired sessions
points.text: A message saying you were logged out and must sign in again is a common trap. Open the site yourself.

points.label: Check before paying
points.text: Before entering card details, confirm that you reached the site yourself and that the address is exactly the one you expect.

screens.key_takeaway: Reach important sites yourself, and let your tools warn you.
